nodes.title: An even touch
nodes.whyImportant: Even key speed gives an even tone, the base for every dynamic you choose.

nodes.title: Playing a crescendo
nodes.whyImportant: A steady crescendo grows note by note instead of jumping.

nodes.title: Playing accents
nodes.whyImportant: Accenting the beat while keeping the rest light makes the metre heard.

nodes.title: Staccato touch
nodes.whyImportant: A crisp staccato lifts each key early without losing the beat.

nodes.title: Legato touch
nodes.whyImportant: Legato means holding each key until the next one sounds, so the line never breaks.

nodes.title: Shaping a phrase
nodes.whyImportant: A phrase played as one breath, joined and gently shaped, sounds like singing.

nodes.title: Melody over accompaniment
nodes.whyImportant: The tune has to sing above the accompaniment, which means one hand plays lighter.

nodes.title: Using the sustain pedal
nodes.whyImportant: The pedal joins sounds the hands cannot hold, and changing it at each chord keeps them clean.

nodes.title: Legato (syncopated) pedalling
nodes.whyImportant: Lifting just after the new chord and pressing again joins the chords with no gap and no blur.

nodes.title: Playing at the marked tempo
nodes.whyImportant: Holding a steady marked tempo is how a tempo term becomes real speed.

edges.rationale: Dynamic levels are the dynamics half of the backbone, spelled out from ppp to fff.
A hairpin is a dynamic mark that moves from one level to another.
Staccato and tenuto are the commonest articulation marks.
A slur is the articulation mark for joined notes.
Tempo terms sit beside dynamics and articulation on the score, in the same Italian.
Ornaments are signs above the notes, read alongside the articulation marks.
Repeat signs are the other score marks a player reads with dynamics and articulation.
Pedal marks shape how notes join, as articulation does.
Dynamics and articulation are read the same way in every instrument part.
A crescendo or diminuendo travels between two dynamic levels.
An accent or sf is louder than the dynamic level around it.
Accents are articulation marks placed on single notes, like staccato dots.
A metronome mark pins the speed that a tempo term only describes.
Rit., accel. and a tempo change the speed the tempo term set.
Character words often come with the tempo term, as in Allegro con brio.
Qualifiers modify tempo terms, as in molto Allegro or poco rit.
Qualifiers modify character words too, as in molto espressivo.
A pause stops the beat for a moment, a local change of tempo.
The trill is one of the ornaments.
The mordents are ornaments.
The turn is an ornament.
Acciaccaturas and appoggiaturas are ornaments written as small notes.
Both decorate a note with its upper and lower neighbours, the turn using both and a mordent one.
D.C. and D.S. are repeats written as words and signs instead of dots.
Open and short score are the two ways the four SATB voices are written.
In open score the tenor part gets its own staff, sometimes in a clef other than treble or bass.
The alto and tenor clefs belong to particular instruments, the viola above all.
A string player takes the notes under a slur in one bow, a wind player in one breath without tonguing.
A crescendo changes loudness gradually just as an accelerando changes speed gradually.
Staccato detaches the notes that legato joins.
Playing a dynamic level means controlling how fast each key goes down.
Playing a crescendo is how a hairpin sign becomes sound.
A smooth crescendo needs the key-speed control an even touch builds.
Playing an accent is how the accent mark becomes sound.
Staccato touch is how the staccato dot becomes sound.
Legato touch is how a slur becomes sound.
A phrase mark is a long slur, and shaping one needs a legato touch.
A phrase is joined from the inside by legato touch.
Balance means playing two dynamic levels at once, one in each hand.
In four-part writing the soprano usually carries the tune, as the melody does over an accompaniment.
Using the pedal is how pedal marks become sound.
The notched pedal line asks for exactly this lift and press at each change.
Legato pedalling is the sustain pedal changed just after each new chord.
Playing at tempo turns a term like Allegro into a speed held steady.
A metronome mark is the speed you play at when it is given.

items.prompt: Which list goes from quietest to loudest?

answer.text: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff
answer.explanation: Right: each step is a little louder, with mp and mf in the middle.

wrong.text: pp, p, mf, mp, f, ff
wrong.explanation: mf (mezzo forte, moderately loud) is louder than mp (mezzo piano, moderately quiet), so they are swapped.

wrong.text: ff, f, mf, mp, p, pp
wrong.explanation: This is the right set but in the other direction, loudest first.

wrong.text: p, pp, mp, mf, ff, f
wrong.explanation: More letters means more extreme: pp is quieter than p and ff louder than f.

items.prompt: What does mp mean?

answer.explanation: Right: mezzo piano, a little louder than p.

wrong.explanation: That is mf, mezzo forte. The p in mp means quiet.
That is pp, pianissimo. Mezzo softens the p, it does not double it.
That is subito piano. Mezzo means moderately.

items.prompt: A hairpin opens out from a point to a wide end. What does it ask for?

answer.explanation: Right: the opening hairpin is a crescendo.

wrong.explanation: That is the closing hairpin, wide end first, a diminuendo.
Hairpins are about loudness. Getting faster is accelerando.
An accent is a small > on one note. A hairpin stretches across many.

items.prompt: Which term means the same as decrescendo?

answer.explanation: Right: both mean getting gradually quieter.

wrong.explanation: Crescendo is the opposite, getting gradually louder.
Ritardando means gradually slower. It changes speed, not loudness.
Morendo means dying away, which fades but also slows. Diminuendo is the exact match.

items.prompt: What does sf (or sfz) under a note mean?

answer.text: A sudden strong accent on that note
answer.explanation: Right: sforzando means forced, one note made suddenly loud.

wrong.text: Play suddenly quiet from here on
wrong.explanation: That is subito piano. Sforzando is a sudden loud accent.
That is crescendo. Sforzando is sudden and on one note.
That is a pause or tenuto. Sforzando is about loudness.

items.prompt: What does fp mean?

answer.explanation: Right: fortepiano, strike the note loud and drop straight to quiet.

wrong.explanation: That is mf. fp is two dynamics in a row.
That would be pf. The letters are read in order, f first.
Pianoforte is the instrument's full name, but under a note fp is a dynamic.

items.prompt: A dot above or below a note head means what?

answer.explanation: Right: a staccato dot shortens the note.

wrong.explanation: That is a dot beside the note head. Above or below it means staccato.

wrong.text: Hold the note its full value
wrong.explanation: That is a tenuto, a short line, not a dot.
That is an accent, a > sign.

items.prompt: A short horizontal line over a note (tenuto) asks for what?

answer.text: Hold the note for its full value, with slight weight
answer.explanation: Right: tenuto means held.

wrong.explanation: That is staccato. Tenuto asks for the opposite.

wrong.text: Join it to the next note of the same pitch
wrong.explanation: That is a tie, a curved line between two notes.

wrong.text: Hold it much longer than written
wrong.explanation: That is a pause (fermata). Tenuto holds the note for its own value.

items.prompt: A curved line joins two notes of the same pitch. What is it?

answer.text: A tie: play once and hold for both values
answer.explanation: Right: a curve between two of the same pitch is a tie.

wrong.text: A slur: play both notes smoothly
wrong.explanation: A slur joins different pitches. On the same pitch the curve is a tie, so you strike only once.
Phrase marks span many notes of different pitches.
A tie means do not strike again.

items.prompt: A slur over four different notes asks for what?

answer.explanation: Right: a slur over different pitches means legato.

wrong.text: Hold the first note through all four
wrong.explanation: That would be a tie, and ties only join the same pitch.
Detached is staccato, the opposite of what a slur asks.
A slur is about joining notes, not loudness.

items.prompt: Which tempo term means at a walking pace?

answer.explanation: Right: andante comes from the Italian for walking.

wrong.explanation: Allegro means quick and lively, faster than walking.
Lento means slow, slower than walking.
Presto means very fast.

items.prompt: Which list goes from slowest to fastest?

answer.explanation: Right: broad, walking, quick, very fast.

wrong.explanation: Largo is slower than Andante, and Presto faster than Allegro.
Right terms, but fastest first.
Andante (walking) is slower than Allegro (quick).

items.prompt: A score shows a crotchet (quarter note) = 60. What does it mean?

answer.text: 60 crotchet beats per minute, one per second
answer.explanation: Right: the number is beats per minute.

wrong.explanation: A metronome mark gives speed, not length.
It counts beats per minute, not bars.
It is 60 per minute, so each lasts one second.

items.prompt: Which metronome mark is fastest?

answer.explanation: Right: more beats per minute means faster.

wrong.explanation: Half as many beats per minute as 120, so slower.
Faster than 60 but slower than 120.
The fewest beats per minute, so the slowest.

items.prompt: What does a tempo mean after a rit.?

answer.text: Go back to the speed before the change
answer.explanation: Right: a tempo means in time again.

wrong.explanation: That would be poco a poco rit. A tempo ends the slowing.
That is ad libitum or rubato.

wrong.text: Speed up beyond the first tempo
wrong.explanation: That would be più mosso or accelerando. A tempo returns to the earlier speed.

items.prompt: Which term means gradually getting faster?

answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.explanation: Rallentando means gradually slower.
Meno mosso means less movement, slower, and at once rather than gradually.
Crescendo is gradually louder, not faster.

items.prompt: What does dolce mean?

answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.explanation: That is maestoso.
That is leggiero.
That is agitato.

items.prompt: Which term means in a singing style?

answer.explanation: Right: cantabile comes from the Italian for to sing.

wrong.explanation: Giocoso means playful, merry.
Sostenuto means sustained. It is close, but singing is cantabile.
Grazioso means gracefully.

items.prompt: What does poco a poco cresc. mean?

answer.explanation: Right: poco a poco means little by little.

wrong.text: Get a little louder, at once
wrong.explanation: That is poco più forte. Poco a poco spreads the change out.
That would be molto cresc.
That would be a crescendo then a diminuendo. Poco a poco only says how gradually.

items.prompt: What does sempre staccato mean?

answer.explanation: Right: sempre means always.

wrong.explanation: That would be senza staccato. Senza means without.
That would be meno staccato.
That would be staccato ma non troppo.

items.prompt: What does a pause sign (fermata) over a note ask for?

answer.text: Hold the note longer than its written value
answer.explanation: Right: how much longer is the player's choice.

wrong.text: Rest for one beat after the note
wrong.explanation: A fermata lengthens the note itself. It adds no rest.
That is staccato, a dot.
That is Fine. A fermata can be mid-piece and the music goes on.

items.prompt: Can a pause sign go over a rest?

answer.text: Yes: the silence is held longer than written
answer.explanation: Right: a pause can lengthen a rest as well as a note.

wrong.explanation: Pauses over rests are common, often at the end of a phrase.

wrong.text: Only at the very end of a piece
wrong.explanation: It is often at the end, but can appear anywhere.

items.prompt: What is an ornament?

answer.text: A sign or small notes that add decoration to a main note
answer.explanation: Right: trills, mordents, turns and grace notes are all ornaments.

wrong.text: A mark that says how loud to play
wrong.explanation: That is a dynamic.

wrong.text: A mark that says how fast to play
wrong.explanation: That is a tempo mark.

wrong.text: A sign that sends you back in the score
wrong.explanation: That is a repeat or D.C. sign.

items.prompt: Which of these is an ornament sign?

answer.explanation: Right: tr is a trill.

wrong.explanation: sf is a sforzando, a dynamic accent.
Ped. is a pedal mark.
D.C. is a repeat instruction.

items.prompt: A trill (tr) on a written C, with no accidental, in C major. Which notes does it alternate?

answer.text: C and D, the note above
answer.explanation: Right: a trill alternates the note with the note a step above, in the key.

wrong.text: C and B, the note below
wrong.explanation: A trill uses the note above. Using the note below is a lower mordent's idea.
A trill moves by step, not by a third.
Only an accidental above the tr sign would raise the upper note.

items.prompt: How is a trill played?

answer.text: A rapid repeated alternation of the note and the one above
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.text: Three notes: the note, the one above, the note
wrong.explanation: That is an upper mordent, one quick alternation.

wrong.text: Four notes winding round the main note
wrong.explanation: That is a turn.

wrong.text: One quick note crushed in before the main note
wrong.explanation: That is an acciaccatura.

items.prompt: An upper mordent on a written E (key of C) is played as what?

answer.explanation: Right: the note, the note above, the note.

wrong.explanation: That is a lower mordent, which goes to the note below. Its sign has a vertical line through it.
That is a turn.

wrong.text: E, F, E, F, E, F
wrong.explanation: That is a trill, longer than a mordent's single alternation.

items.prompt: How do you tell a lower mordent sign from an upper one?

answer.text: The lower mordent has a short vertical line through it
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.text: The lower mordent is written below the note
wrong.explanation: Both are written above the note. The line through it marks the lower one.

wrong.text: The lower mordent is a turned-over S shape
wrong.explanation: That is a turn sign.

wrong.text: The lower mordent has tr in front
wrong.explanation: tr marks a trill.

items.prompt: A turn over a written D (key of C) is played as which four notes?

answer.explanation: Right: the note above, the note, the note below, the note.

wrong.explanation: That starts below. A plain turn starts on the note above. The one starting below is an inverted turn.
That is an upper mordent, three notes.
That is the start of a trill.

items.prompt: Which notes does a turn use around the written note?

answer.text: The note above and the note below
answer.explanation: Right: it winds around the note on both sides.

wrong.explanation: Using only the note above is a trill or upper mordent.
Using only the note below is a lower mordent.

wrong.text: The notes a third above and below
wrong.explanation: A turn moves by step.

items.prompt: A small note with a stroke through its stem, before a main note. What is it?

answer.text: An acciaccatura: crushed in as quickly as possible
answer.explanation: Right: the stroke marks the acciaccatura.

wrong.text: An appoggiatura: leans and takes time from the main note
wrong.explanation: The appoggiatura has no stroke and takes real time, often half the main note.
A mordent is a sign above the note, not a small note.
Staccato is a dot.

items.prompt: An appoggiatura comes before an undotted minim. How long does it usually last?

answer.explanation: Right: an appoggiatura usually takes half the main note's value.

wrong.explanation: That is the acciaccatura.
Two thirds is the usual rule before a dotted note.

wrong.text: No time: it is played with the main note
wrong.explanation: An appoggiatura takes time from the main note and delays it.

items.prompt: A passage has a 1st time bar and a 2nd time bar. How do you play it?

answer.text: Play the 1st time bar, repeat, then skip it and play the 2nd
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.explanation: The 1st time bar is skipped on the repeat.
The 1st time bar is played the first time through.
The order is 1st, then repeat, then 2nd.

items.prompt: Two dots before a double barline mean what?

answer.text: Go back to the matching start repeat sign, or the beginning if there is none
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.explanation: A plain final barline or Fine ends it. Dots mean repeat.
That is a pause.
That is the coda sign.

items.prompt: What does D.C. al Fine mean?

answer.text: Go back to the beginning and play to Fine
answer.explanation: Right: da capo means from the head.

wrong.text: Go back to the sign and play to Fine
wrong.explanation: That is D.S. al Fine. D.S. means from the sign.

wrong.text: Go back to the beginning and play to the coda
wrong.explanation: That is D.C. al Coda.
That is Fine on its own.

items.prompt: In D.S. al Coda, what is the segno?

answer.text: The sign you go back to
answer.explanation: Right: dal segno means from the sign, a slanted S with dots.

wrong.text: The ending section you jump to
wrong.explanation: That is the coda, marked with a circle and cross.
That is Fine.
That is the fermata.

items.prompt: Under a piano part you see Ped. and later *. What do they mean?

answer.text: Press the sustain pedal at Ped. and lift it at *
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.text: Press the soft pedal, then lift it
wrong.explanation: The soft pedal is una corda. Ped. means the sustain pedal.
These are pedal marks, not dynamics.

wrong.text: Lift at Ped. and press at *
wrong.explanation: It is the other way round.

items.prompt: What does una corda mean?

answer.explanation: Right: una corda means one string, and tre corde lifts it.

wrong.explanation: The sustain pedal is marked Ped.

wrong.text: Play one note at a time
wrong.explanation: Corda means string, the piano's strings under the soft pedal.
That would be mano sinistra or mano destra.

items.prompt: In SATB, which two voices are written on the treble staff in short score?

answer.explanation: Right: soprano and alto on the treble, tenor and bass on the bass staff.

wrong.explanation: Tenor goes on the bass staff in short score.
Alto is on the treble staff but tenor is on the bass.
They share the bass staff.

items.prompt: In short score, which voices have stems pointing up?

answer.explanation: Right: the upper voice on each staff has stems up.

wrong.explanation: Alto shares the treble staff with soprano, so its stems go down.
These are the lower voices on their staves, so stems go down.
Stems show which voice is which, so each staff has one up and one down.

items.prompt: What is open score for SATB?

answer.text: Each voice on its own staff, four staves
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.text: Two staves, two voices on each
wrong.explanation: That is short score.

wrong.text: One staff with all four voices
wrong.explanation: Four voices on one staff is not a standard layout.

wrong.text: Only the soprano line with chord symbols
wrong.explanation: That is a lead sheet.

items.prompt: In open score, the tenor part is often in a treble clef with a small 8 below. What does it mean?

answer.text: It sounds an octave lower than written
answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.text: It sounds an octave higher than written
wrong.explanation: The 8 below means lower. An 8 above would mean higher.
The 8 is about octave, not repeats.
Time signatures are written after the clef and key, not on it.

items.prompt: Which family does the oboe belong to?

answer.explanation: Right: the oboe is a double-reed woodwind.

wrong.explanation: Brass instruments are played by buzzing the lips, like the trumpet.
Strings, like the violin, are bowed or plucked.
Percussion is struck, like the timpani.

items.prompt: Which instrument sounds an octave lower than written?

answer.explanation: Right: its part is written an octave above where it sounds.

wrong.explanation: The piccolo sounds an octave higher than written.
It sounds a major 2nd lower, not an octave.
The violin sounds as written.

items.prompt: In the alto clef, which note is on the middle line?

answer.explanation: Right: the alto clef centres on middle C.

wrong.explanation: B is the middle line of the treble clef.
D is the middle line of the bass clef.
In the tenor clef, A is on the middle line, since middle C is one line up.

items.prompt: Which instrument reads mainly in the alto clef?

answer.explanation: Right.

wrong.explanation: The cello reads bass clef, and tenor clef for higher notes.
The violin reads treble clef.
The trombone reads bass clef, and tenor clef for higher notes.

items.prompt: Ode to Joy (Beethoven), right hand, bars 1-4. Play every note at the same mezzo forte, with no note louder or quieter than the rest.
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, first four bars. Keep the touch even and quiet, piano, on every note, the repeated ones too.
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, first two bars. Start piano and grow steadily to forte by the last note, a little louder on each one.
Ode to Joy (Beethoven), right hand, bars 1-2. Make a smooth crescendo from p to f, then hold the forte.
Minuet in G (attributed to Petzold), right hand, bars 1-4. Accent the first beat of each bar and keep beats 2 and 3 light.
Clementi, Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1, bars 1-2. Give each bar's first beat a clear accent and keep the other notes lighter.
Burgmüller, L'arabesque, left hand, bars 1-4. Play the chords staccato: short, light and exactly on the beat.
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, first two bars. Play every note staccato, bouncing off the keys, and keep the beat steady.
Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata, 1st movement, right-hand triplets, bars 1-3. Hold each key until the next goes down, so the triplets flow without a gap. No pedal.
Chopin, Nocturne in E flat Op. 9 No. 2, right-hand melody from bar 3. Join every note to the next with your fingers alone: no gaps, no pedal.
Chopin, Nocturne in E flat Op. 9 No. 2, the opening phrase in the right hand. Shape it as one breath: joined throughout, rising a little to the top note and easing off at the end.
Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, the first melody phrase in the right hand. Play it as one long, joined line that swells gently and fades.
Mozart, Sonata in C K. 545, 1st movement, bars 1-2. Let the right-hand melody sing over a quiet, even left-hand Alberti bass.
Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, from where the melody enters. Keep the left-hand bass and chords soft and let the right-hand tune float above them.
Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata, 1st movement, left-hand octaves, bars 1-4. Change the pedal at each new octave: lift as the new one sounds, then press again.
Chopin, Prelude in E minor Op. 28 No. 4, left-hand chords. Change the pedal each time the harmony changes, and keep it down through the repeated chords.
Debussy, Clair de lune, left-hand thirds from bar 1. Use legato pedalling: lift just after each new third sounds and press again at once, so nothing blurs and nothing breaks.
Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata, 1st movement, left hand, bars 5-9. Change the pedal just after each new chord or octave, with no gap in the sound.
Clementi, Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1 (Allegro), bars 1-2, at crotchet = 100. Hold the tempo steady with the click from the first note to the last.
Minuet in G (attributed to Petzold), right hand, bars 1-4, at crotchet = 100. Keep every beat exactly with the click, no rushing.
